issues.legal_issue: A requisitioning authority releasing premises from requisition may direct the occupant to vacate so that possession can be restored to the person entitled to receive it.
material_facts: The premises were requisitioned for the appellant and allotted to him.
The authority had taken vacant possession of the premises from the landlord.
When the premises were de-requisitioned, the appellant remained in occupation and the Collector directed him to vacate so possession could be delivered to the landlord.
issues.conclusion: The Collector was competent, and required, to direct the appellant to vacate and to restore possession to the landlord when releasing the premises from requisition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 9(1)–(4) and 9(7) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, the State Government may release requisitioned land, specify the person to whom possession is to be given, and direct the person in possession and any other occupant to deliver possession for that purpose. Section 11 provides for an authorised officer to take possession in the circumstances specified in the Act. No earlier case is relied on.

rule.if: requisition_release_proceeding and property_was_requisitioned and authority_took_vacant_possession and occupant_remains_in_property

predicates.requisition_release_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the release of property from a public authority's requisition.
predicates.property_was_requisitioned: A public authority requisitioned the property.
predicates.authority_took_vacant_possession: The public authority took vacant possession of the property from the person who supplied it.
predicates.occupant_remains_in_property: An occupant remains in the property when the authority releases it from requisition.
predicates.authority_may_order_occupant_to_vacate_a: The authority may direct the occupant to vacate so possession can be restored to the person entitled to receive it.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns release of requisitioned property that the authority took vacant, and an occupant remains there, the authority may order the occupant to vacate and restore possession.

issues.legal_issue: Withdrawal of a later notification concerning an area does not release property that was lawfully requisitioned before the withdrawal.
material_facts: An earlier notification continued to apply to the area containing the premises.
A later notification again specified the municipal area, and the Government subsequently rescinded that later notification.
The premises had been lawfully requisitioned before the later notification was rescinded.
issues.conclusion: Rescinding the later notification did not release the premises from requisition; at most, it could prevent further action under the relevant requisitioning power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(3) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, permits the State Government to direct by notification that provisions of the Act cease to extend to an area. The Court held that withdrawal of the later, duplicative area notification did not undo an existing lawful requisition; even if it prevented further action under Section 6, it did not itself release property already requisitioned. No earlier case is relied on.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_existing_requisiti: The proceeding concerns whether property remains subject to an existing requisition.
predicates.property_was_lawfully_requisitioned_befo: The property was lawfully requisitioned before a later area notification was withdrawn.
predicates.later_area_notification_was_withdrawn: A later notification concerning the area was withdrawn.
predicates.withdrawal_does_not_release_existing_req: Withdrawal of the later notification does not itself release property already requisitioned.

issues.definition: If a proceeding challenges an existing requisition, the property was lawfully requisitioned before a later area notification was withdrawn, and that notification was withdrawn, the withdrawal does not release the existing requisition.

issues.legal_issue: A requisitioning authority and a court exercising extraordinary writ jurisdiction do not determine disputed private tenancy rights when possession is restored on de-requisitioning.
material_facts: The appellant relied on the landlord's earlier treatment of him as a tenant and asserted private tenancy rights after de-requisitioning.
The Collector's order directed vacation as part of releasing the requisitioned premises and restoring possession.
The appellant challenged the order through a writ petition, while the Court noted that private rights between the occupant and landlord had a different forum for determination.
issues.conclusion: The Collector was not required to decide whether a private tenancy arrangement existed, and the disputed rights were not to be determined in the writ proceeding; they could be pursued in a separate forum.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 of the Constitution confers extraordinary writ jurisdiction, but the Court held that a dispute over private rights between an occupant and landlord was not for decision by the Collector as part of de-requisitioning or by the High Court in that writ proceeding. No earlier case is relied on.

predicates.writ_challenges_de_requisition_order: A writ proceeding challenges an order made in connection with de-requisitioning property.
predicates.private_tenancy_rights_are_disputed: The occupant and landlord have disputed claims about private tenancy rights.
predicates.authority_is_restoring_requisitioned_pro: The authority is restoring property to the person entitled to receive it after requisition ends.
predicates.private_tenancy_rights_require_separate_: The disputed private tenancy rights must be determined in a separate forum rather than in the de-requisitioning decision or the writ proceeding.

issues.definition: When a writ challenges a de-requisitioning order, private tenancy rights are disputed, and the authority is restoring the property, those private rights require a separate forum.
